deep.reconstruction:
Purpose: first-order corrections that turn geocentric (ephemeris) right ascension and declination into apparent topocentric, refracted places. The next page applies them to the Sun on 1809 May 11 at Göttingen.

Notation (Gauss): α right ascension, δ declination, φ latitude (Polhöhe), h hour angle (counted westward), ρ refraction at 45° altitude, ϖ horizontal parallax.

[Implicit steps, mine]
1. Zenith distance z: cos z = sinφ sinδ + cosφ cosδ cos h.
2. Parallactic angle q: sin z sin q = cosφ sin h and sin z cos q = sinφ cosδ − cosφ sinδ cos h.

Refraction:
3. Model: refraction raises the star toward the zenith by R = ρ tan z. This is the simple tangent law; ρ is the value at z = 45°, since tan 45° = 1.
4. A displacement R toward the zenith gives Δδ = R cos q and Δh = −R sin q / cosδ.
5. Since α = sidereal time − h, Δα = +R sin q / cosδ.
6. Substituting R = ρ sin z / cos z:
   Δα_ref = ρ cosφ sin h / [cosδ (sinφ sinδ + cosφ cosδ cos h)]
   Δδ_ref = ρ (sinφ cosδ − cosφ sinδ cos h) / (sinφ sinδ + cosφ cosδ cos h).
   These are Gauss's first-table entries.

Parallax:
7. Parallax depresses the body away from the zenith by ϖ sin z. Spherical Earth, first order.
8. Hence Δα_par = −ϖ cosφ sin h / cosδ and Δδ_par = −ϖ (sinφ cosδ − cosφ sinδ cos h).

Auxiliary angle θ, with tan θ = tan φ / cos h:
9. Put k = sinφ / sinθ = cosφ cos h / cosθ, so that sinφ = k sinθ and cosφ cos h = k cosθ. [mine]
10. Then cos z = k cos(θ−δ) and sinφ cosδ − cosφ sinδ cos h = k sin(θ−δ). [mine]
11. Results:
   Δδ_ref = ρ tan(θ−δ)
   Δα_ref = ρ cosφ sin h / (cosδ · k cos(θ−δ)) = ρ cosθ tan h / (cosδ cos(θ−δ))
   Δα_par unchanged
   Δδ_par = −ϖ k sin(θ−δ) = −ϖ sinφ sin(θ−δ) / sinθ.
   These are exactly the second-table entries. The auxiliary angle makes them convenient for logarithmic computation.

Next-page check:
- log ρ = 1.7333 gives ρ ≈ 54.1″.
- With h = 322°18′ (east of the meridian), tan h and sin h are negative.
- This gives refraction −30.5″ in RA and +45.5″ in Dec, and parallax corrections +3.4″ and −5.1″. All signs agree with the formulas.
errors: No errors in the formulas; all four entries of both tables are correct to first order.
Unstated approximations: tangent refraction law; spherical Earth (no geocentric latitude or radius); parallax and refraction treated as small first-order quantities (terms in ϖ², ρ² neglected).
Quadrant of θ not specified. It must be taken with sinθ of the same sign as sinφ (0<θ<180° in the north), so that k > 0. This is implicit; in the worked example θ ≈ 58°, which is correct.
Corrections are in arc; RA is used in degrees, which is consistent with the next page.

results.what: Effect of atmospheric refraction (R = ρ tan z) on right ascension and declination via the parallactic angle
results.modern_name: Differential refraction in equatorial coordinates (first-order refraction correction to α, δ)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century spherical astronomy (Bradley, Lalande, Delambre; later Bessel's Tabulae Regiomontanae)

results.what: Effect of diurnal (horizontal) parallax on α and δ
results.modern_name: Diurnal parallax in right ascension and declination

results.what: Auxiliary angle tanθ = tanφ/cos h reducing the formulas to products suited to logarithms (Δδ_ref = ρ tan(θ−δ), etc.)
results.usually_credited_to: Common computational device of the period (Delambre, Gauss, Bessel, Encke)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard first-order formulas of practical spherical astronomy around 1809, written in a convenient logarithmic form with a usual auxiliary angle. They are correct and neatly organized, but there is nothing beyond contemporary textbook practice.
